case_study_insert.main_stem: Quill & Muse Boutique (QMB) is a sole trader business in the luxury online accessories sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2016 by Seraphina Quill in Paris, the business sells handmade scarves and bags through its own website and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. QMB plans to invest $260,000 in a digital photography studio and an automated stock-control system, financed by a $150,000 bank loan and $110,000 of the owner's savings. It has fixed costs of $96,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $42.00, and sells 8,000 units a year. QMB faces two operational problems: the return rate has reached 12.1% because of sizing complaints and stock-outs are losing sales.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — Q4 2026: A questionnaire of 300 online accessories buyers found 44% had returned an item for sizing reasons and 73% consult product photographs before purchase. The observed return rate in Q4 was 12.1%, up from 8.4%, and 52 complaints were logged about unclear product images. Stock-outs affected 9% of listed scarves. Focus groups of 24 shoppers found 68% would buy more if more angles were shown. Hiring a freelance photographer costs $12 per item, while training an existing employee in product photography costs $600 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Quill & Muse Boutique as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2027): (1) Base interest rates have risen from 4.75% to 5.5%, increasing loan interest for small businesses. (2) The national minimum wage will rise 6.2% from $13.14 to $13.95 an hour from April 2027, affecting the cost of the 16-strong workforce. (3) Courier and packing material costs have increased 10.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on luxury online accessories grew 4.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: QMB plans to fund part of its $260,000 photography studio with a $150,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for QMB of using $110,000 of the owner's savings instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $110,000 of the owner's savings avoids extra interest and repayment obligations, which protects QMB's cash flow while fixed costs already stand at $96,000 a year. The money not borrowed can instead fund the automated stock-control system, tackling the 9% of scarves affected by stock-outs, without increasing the burden of the $150,000 bank loan or forcing the $42.00 selling price higher.

Point 2: Owner savings carry no collateral or repossession risk, so Seraphina Quill's luxury accessories business is not exposed if the studio fails to reduce the 12.1% return rate. As a sole trader she also keeps full control: no lender can set conditions on how the website or photography is run, so decisions can be made quickly under the hierarchical structure. Committing her own savings also demonstrates personal commitment to suppliers and to the 16-strong workforce when the business invests $260,000 in new capacity. Keeping $110,000 of savings invested also reduces the risk that a fall in sales below the 4,000-unit break-even point leaves her unable to meet loan instalments.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to QMB's funding decision and costs.

questions.question_text: QMB is relaunching its scarf and bag range online. Consider fashion magazine print advertising, social media influencer marketing, or search engine advertising. Which should QMB choose to promote the relaunch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Fashion magazine print advertising: A glossy magazine suits a Paris luxury brand and can convey status through high-quality images. However, print is expensive, slow to book and hard to measure, and a national readership would include few of the 300 surveyed online accessories buyers; it also cannot respond quickly to the 9% stock-out problem.

Social media influencer marketing: Influencers can show scarves and bags in many angles and outfits, which matters because 73% of buyers consult photographs and 68% said more angles would increase purchases. Content can target luxury accessories audiences and link straight to the website. The disadvantages are that influencer fees vary, results take time, and a poorly matched partner could damage the brand image behind the $42.00 price.

Search engine advertising: Paid search reaches shoppers already looking for handmade accessories, so it converts strongly and can be switched on or off as stock allows, which helps when 9% of scarves are out of stock. It is measurable within the $260,000 investment, but it depends on text rather than the photography that 73% of buyers consult, and popular keywords can be costly.

Recommendation: QMB should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by limited search advertising. Influencer content best exploits the new photography studio and answers the 68% who want more angles, potentially lowering the 12.1% return rate driven by sizing complaints. Search ads alone show too little of the product, while magazine advertising is rejected as slow, expensive and unmeasurable for a 16-person online business; search can be used as a low-cost supplement for high-intent buyers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of QMB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of QMB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazines and search-only advertising lose.

questions.question_text: QMB's return rate is 12.1% and stock-outs are losing sales. Explain two benefits for QMB of its autocratic leadership style within a hierarchical structure.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Seraphina Quill decide quickly how to fix the 12.1% return rate, for example by ordering clearer size guides without waiting for committee approval. In a hierarchical structure the instruction passes down a short chain to the workforce of 16, so the 52 complaints about unclear images can be acted on immediately, protecting the $42.00 selling price and the luxury image.

Point 2: Clear, central decisions suit the stock-control problem: with 9% of scarves out of stock, one owner can set reorder levels for the new automated system and hold staff accountable for updating records. Fast decisions also limit the damage from fixed costs of $96,000 a year, because the 8,000 units sold must keep covering costs; when a single owner decides, the $260,000 studio investment can be redirected towards the best-selling lines without delay. Decisive action is valuable while returns and stock-outs are both rising.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to QMB's returns, stock-outs and structure.

questions.question_text: QMB wants clearer product images to cut its 12.1% return rate. Consider hiring a freelance photographer or training an existing employee in product photography. Which should QMB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Hiring a freelance photographer: At $12 per item this is a variable cost that rises only with the photographs needed, so QMB avoids a fixed salary and can demand professional quality immediately. Given that 73% of buyers consult photographs and 52 complaints concern unclear images, expert work could quickly reduce the 12.1% return rate. The weakness is that $12 on each of 8,000 units would be $96,000 a year (8,000 × $12), equal to the whole annual fixed cost, if every item needed a new shoot, and freelancers may not be available when stock changes.

Training an existing employee: A $600 course for one of the workforce of 16 creates an in-house skill that can be reused, is cheap against the $260,000 studio investment, and fits the hierarchical structure because the owner can set standards directly. The staff member can reshoot items whenever the 9% stock-out problem is fixed. Training takes time, however, and early photos may be poorer, which matters when 68% of focus-group shoppers said more angles would make them buy more.

Decision: QMB should train an existing employee first and use a freelance photographer only for the highest-value lines. The $600 cost is predictable and builds a lasting capability, whereas hiring at $12 per item could reach $96,000 a year and is rejected as the main approach because it offers no lasting skill and depends on outside availability. A short freelance commission can set the visual standard while the employee trains, combining speed with long-term control. She should set a clear standard for the images, since 52 complaints about unclear pictures and a 12.1% return rate show that the current photography is already costing sales.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to QMB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of QMB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of QMB with a well-justified decision covering cost, quality and flexibility.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how QMB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $96,000 ÷ ($42.00 − $18.00) = $96,000 ÷ $24.00 = 4,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $42.00 − $18.00 = $24.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways QMB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even output of 4,000 units against sales of 8,000 units gives a margin of safety of 4,000 units, so Seraphina Quill can see how much demand can fall before the $260,000 studio investment stops paying.
2. Contribution per unit of $24.00 lets QMB judge a discount to shift slow stock: a $4.00 price cut would leave $20.00 contribution, still covering the $96,000 fixed costs if volume held.
3. The 4,000-unit break-even point sets a sales floor for servicing the $150,000 bank loan, so the owner can decide whether to cut the $12-per-item photography spend without endangering repayments.
4. Unit cost of $30.00 ($96,000 ÷ 8,000 units = $12.00 plus $18.00 variable cost) can be compared each month to detect the effect of the 12.1% return rate and the 9% stock-out rate on profitability.

questions.model_answer: (i) break-even output = 4,000 units | (ii) contribution per unit = $24.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 4,000 units against 8,000-unit sales; discount testing on $24.00 contribution; servicing the $150,000 bank loan; unit cost of $30.00 to monitor the 12.1% return rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QMB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has QMB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.25 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.85 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $40,000 + $40,000 + $20,000 = $100,000; 2025 current assets = $32,000 + $48,000 + $20,000 = $100,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $100,000 in 2024 and $80,000 in 2025 gives the first pair of figures. Removing stock leaves $60,000 in 2024 and $68,000 in 2025, and dividing those by the same liabilities gives the second pair.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly improved. The first ratio rose from 1.00 to 1.25 solely because current liabilities fell from $100,000 to $80,000 while current assets stayed at $100,000, giving more room to meet obligations on the $150,000 bank loan. The second ratio improved from 0.60 to 0.85, showing less reliance on the $32,000 of inventories, which is useful when a 12.1% return rate may leave scarves hard to sell. Nevertheless, cash stayed flat at $20,000 while trade receivables rose from $40,000 to $48,000, so much of the improvement rests on customers paying on time; a sole trader with fixed costs of $96,000 a year has little buffer if they do not.

Conclusion: QMB's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the rise in the second measure shows the change is not just stock-based. The main weakness is the flat cash balance and growing receivables, so the owner should chase payments before committing more of the $260,000 studio budget.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether QMB's position improved.

questions.question_text: QMB is considering charging a higher price of $42.00 for its handmade scarves. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QMB of this pricing decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The $42.00 price supports the luxury positioning of handmade Paris accessories and helps fund the $260,000 photography studio; with contribution of $24.00 a unit, each sale adds strongly towards fixed costs of $96,000. Because 73% of buyers consult photographs, better images can justify the higher price and 68% said more angles would encourage purchases, so the premium can be defended through the new studio rather than a discount.

Disadvantage: The 12.1% return rate, driven by sizing complaints and 44% of survey respondents having returned an item, shows that customers already perceive a mismatch between expectation and product; a higher price may make them less forgiving and push returns higher. With variable costs of $18.00 a unit, lost sales also mean lost contribution, and a 9% stock-out rate means QMB cannot always supply buyers willing to pay the premium. The business should test the price on one line first. It should also check whether the 68% of focus-group shoppers who want more angles would accept the premium once the new studio improves the images.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to QMB's research, costs and return rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 10.4% rise in courier and packing material costs will affect QMB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If QMB's $150,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $150,000 = $1,125 a year (0.0075 × $150,000). That is small relative to fixed costs of $96,000 a year and can be eliminated by fixing the rate, so this is the least serious change. Higher rates might also reduce luxury spending, although the bulletin reports that spending on luxury online accessories actually grew 4.2%.

Minimum wage rise (6.2%, to $13.95 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 16 but no hours or pay rates, so a defensible annual wage total cannot be calculated. Qualitatively, the rise raises the cost of running the website operation and the photography studio and cannot be avoided. Its effect depends on the 8,000 units sold: if the 12.1% return rate persists, the $24.00 contribution per unit will absorb the increase, but if the new images cut returns, productivity improves and the impact is muted.

Courier and packing inflation (10.4%): Delivery is essential to an online accessories business, and 73% of buyers consult photographs before purchase, so service quality cannot simply be cut. Because the insert does not decompose the $18.00 variable cost into delivery and materials, only a bound can be shown: if all of it rose by 10.4%, that would add 0.104 × $18.00 = $1.87 per unit and, at 8,000 units, $14,976 a year (8,000 × $1.87). Even a fraction of that would reduce the $24.00 contribution.

Conclusion: The 10.4% rise in courier and packing costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every unit, threatens far more annual cost than the $1,125 interest change, and cannot be avoided by fixing a loan rate; the wage rise is real but unquantifiable from the insert. QMB should renegotiate courier contracts and use its $42.00 price and better photography to protect contribution while watching the 12.1% return rate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to QMB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on QMB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of QMB with a well-justified judgement that delivery cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
